15.title: the rule that keeps turning up
15.hook: the rule that keeps turning up
15.tomorrow: start with the person in the mirror
15.howItsDone: The golden rule is taught in many religious and ethical settings: Jewish teaching often recalls Hillel's saying, Christian teaching the Sermon on the Mount, Confucian teaching the Analects, and families often pass it to children as an early rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gratitude, and thank you anyway. Week three turns toward other people. Day fifteen.

A playground, right after somebody grabbed something that wasn't theirs. A grown-up crouches down and says it: treat people the way you want to be treated. Plenty of kids hear it before they can read. It's so familiar it sounds like nothing. But here's the strange part. You can find it in ancient China, in Jewish law, in the sayings of the rabbis, in the words of Jesus, in India's great epic, in Greek writers. It turns up on path after path.
screen: `TREAT PEOPLE THE WAY YOU WANT TO BE TREATED.` → `CHINA. THE BIBLE. INDIA. GREECE.` → `PATH AFTER PATH.`

segments.voice: Start in China. A student asks Confucius if there's one word you could live by your whole life. In an old translation, Confucius answers: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Notice it's a don't. The Hebrew Bible, in among laws about harvests and fair wages, says to love your neighbor as yourself. Centuries later, a man asks the rabbi Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel says, roughly: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it. Then Jesus puts it as a do: "all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." India's great epic has a version. So does the Greek orator Isocrates. Did each path arrive at it on its own? Nobody can say for sure who heard what from whom. What's clear is that it keeps turning up, and each tradition keeps it in its own place. For Confucius it's one word for a whole life. For Hillel, a summary that sends you back to study. For Jesus, the law and the prophets in a sentence. And notice where the rule starts: with you. What you don't want. What you would want. It asks you to use your own heart as a map of someone else's.
screen: `CONFUCIUS: RECIPROCITY.` · `HILLEL: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.` · `JESUS: DO YE EVEN SO TO THEM.` · `YOUR HEART AS A MAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. From today the bell gives you a little longer, about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone you'll see today. Then ask: if I were them, today, what would I want? Maybe to be listened to. Maybe to be left alone for a bit. Maybe just a real hello. Let the answer settle. You don't have to do anything with it yet. Just know it.
The golden rule. What you'd want, given. What you'd hate, held back. Found on path after path. Fifteenth word.
Your line: be good to people. Your own heart already knows the map. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 15 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: START WITH THE PERSON IN THE MIRROR.`

16.title: start with the person in the mirror
16.hook: start with the person in the mirror
16.tomorrow: do something for someone with no receipt
16.howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) meditation, practitioners often begin by silently wishing themselves well with a few short phrases, then extend the same wishes to a friend, a stranger, a difficult person and finally all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the golden rule, your own heart as a map of someone else's. Today, the one person the map tends to leave out.

A friend burns the dinner. Misses a deadline. Says the wrong thing at the wrong moment. What comes out of your mouth? Usually something like: hey, it happens, you're tired, it's fine. Now flip it. You burn the dinner. What does the voice inside say then? Sometimes it's a voice nobody would be allowed to use on a friend. Idiot. Of course you did. Typical. One old tradition insists kindness starts with the person in the mirror.
screen: `WHAT YOU SAY TO A FRIEND.` → `WHAT YOU SAY TO YOURSELF.` → `START WITH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: In the early Buddhist teachings there's a word, metta. It's usually translated loving-kindness, but it comes from the Pali word for friend. Metta is friendliness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does. One short Buddhist discourse describes it with a picture: the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, a person can grow a heart like that toward every living being. Here's the surprise. The Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa wrote a long guide to meditation, and when he explains how to practice metta, he says not to start with everyone. Start with yourself. Wish yourself well first, with phrases like may I be happy, may I be free from trouble. Then extend it outward: to someone dear, to someone neutral, and eventually to someone difficult. His reasoning is plain. You know from the inside that you want to be happy. That makes you the example: everyone else wants the same. Remember yesterday's line from the Hebrew Bible: "love thy neighbour as thyself." Those last two words carry a quiet assumption: that there's some care for yourself to measure by. Modern research points somewhere similar. The psychologist Kristin Neff studies self-compassion: treating your own failures the way you'd treat a friend's. A common worry is that being kind to yourself will make you lazy. In one set of studies, people nudged to be gentler about a mistake were more willing to own it, and put more effort into doing better. Some people feel they don't even deserve to sit, because of something they've done. If that's you: feeling bad about harm means your conscience works, and practice is how people learn to do less of it. Kindness isn't a reward for getting it right. It's where you start.
screen: `METTA: THE FRIEND WORD.` · `START WITH YOURSELF, THEN OUTWARD.` · `AS THYSELF.` · `GENTLE WITH MISTAKES, MORE LIKELY TO TRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture yourself the way a good friend might see you right now: tired, trying, doing your best with the day you've had. On each breath out, say quietly inside: may I be at ease. If it feels strange or even a little silly, that's normal. Say it anyway.
Kindness. Wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with the one in the mirror. Sixteenth word.
Your line: may I be at ease. It's the sentence you'd give a friend, turned around. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DO SOMETHING FOR SOMEONE WITH NO RECEIPT.`

17.title: do something for someone with no receipt
17.hook: do something for someone with no receipt
17.howItsDone: Sikhs volunteer in the langar, the free kitchen of the gurdwara; Jewish and Christian teaching both honor giving that the receiver, or the giver's own circle, never hears about; and Hindu teaching speaks of acting without attachment to reward.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kindness, starting with the one in the mirror. Today, kindness with no name on it.

A good deed can come with a little receipt attached. I drove them to the airport. I remembered her birthday. I did the dishes, again. The receipts tend to print themselves. And sometimes the receipt wants to be seen: a thank-you, a mention, a like. Today is about the other kind of giving: no thanks, no credit, maybe nobody even knowing it was you. Four traditions have a lot to say about it.
screen: `THE RECEIPT PRINTS ITSELF.` → `A THANK-YOU, A MENTION, A LIKE.` → `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Jesus talks about giving to the poor, and says to do it so quietly that, in the King James wording, you "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Your own other hand shouldn't find out. The Jewish scholar Maimonides set out eight levels of giving, from grudging to generous. Near the very top: the giver and the receiver don't know each other's names. And at the top itself: helping someone so they won't need help again, with a gift, a loan, a partnership, a job. In Sikh tradition the word is seva, selfless service, and you can see it in the gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship. Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen where anyone, of any faith or none, sits and eats together. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the kitchen feeds a vast number of people every day, served by volunteers whose names the people eating will never learn. And Hindu teaching has a famous line about acting without clinging to the fruits of the action: do the work well, and let go of what it earns you. The reasons differ. For Jesus, the Father sees what's done in secret. For Maimonides, the poor person's dignity matters. In the Hindu line, the doer lets go of the reward. They don't mean the same thing by it. But each of them treats the receipt as the part to throw away.
screen: `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.` · `MAIMONIDES' LADDER OF GIVING.` · `SEVA AND THE FREE KITCHEN.` · `LET GO OF THE FRUITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about seventy-five seconds, think of one small thing you could do for someone where nobody would know it was you. Putting a shopping cart back. Refilling the coffee. Paying for something quietly. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it and walking away, no thank-you. Notice what that feels like.
Service. Doing good for someone else, without keeping the receipt. Seventeenth word.
Your line: no receipt. A good deed is already finished the moment it's done. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU'RE NOT THE ONLY ONE.`

18.title: you're not the only one
18.hook: you're not the only one; the room at sunset
18.tomorrow: look at something bigger than you today
18.howItsDone: Many traditions meet loneliness with shared practice at set hours, so that people praying or sitting alone know others are doing the same, and with care for those on their own, such as visiting the sick and the isolated.

segments.voice: Yesterday: service, and no receipt. Today, a feeling that's very good at hiding.

You can feel it in a full room. At a party where everyone seems to know everyone. In a group chat that's buzzing with jokes you're not part of. At 2am, awake, when the whole building seems to be asleep but you. Loneliness is strange that way. It isn't about how many people are near you. It's the feeling that nobody is really with you. And one of its cruelest tricks is convincing you that you're the only one who feels it. You're not. Not even close.
screen: `A FULL ROOM, AND STILL ALONE.` → `AWAKE AT 2AM.` → `YOU'RE NOT THE ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: In 2023, the Surgeon General of the United States issued a formal public health advisory about loneliness, the kind usually saved for things like smoking. It reported that about half of American adults said they'd experienced it. Half. Which means that in almost any room, a good number of the people are quietly feeling what you feel. The old texts knew this ache. Near the start of the Bible, before anything has gone wrong in the garden, God looks at the first human and says, in the King James wording: "It is not good that the man should be alone." It's the first thing in the whole story called not good. Old prayers are full of people saying so, out loud: turn to me, for I am alone. The night before he dies, Jesus asks his closest friends to stay awake with him while he prays, and they fall asleep. Many traditions have noticed that being alone and being lonely aren't the same thing. The same hour on your own can feel like a punishment or like a rest. Monks and hermits choose solitude. Nobody chooses loneliness. Now, the room at sunset. At this hour, somewhere, a family is lighting candles. Someone is unrolling a prayer mat. Someone in a monastery is singing the evening prayers, someone is sitting on a cushion, someone is just stopping on a balcony to watch the light. You can't see them. They can't see you. But you're all doing the same small, brave thing at the same kind of hour. The room is full.
screen: `HALF OF ADULTS SAID THEY'D FELT IT.` · `THE FIRST THING CALLED NOT GOOD.` · `ALONE ISN'T THE SAME AS LONELY.` · `THE ROOM AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about seventy-five seconds, picture the room at sunset. Somewhere, someone lighting a candle. Someone kneeling. Someone sitting just like you, a little tired, stopping anyway. You don't know their names. On each breath out, let yourself be one of them. If loneliness is heavy today, let it be here too. It's allowed in the room.
Loneliness. The feeling that nobody is with you, and one of the most widely shared feelings there is. Eighteenth word.
Your line: the room is full. And if the loneliness is heavy today, telling one person is a brave and good first step. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOK AT SOMETHING BIGGER THAN YOU TODAY.`

19.title: look at something bigger than you today
19.hook: look at something bigger than you today
19.tomorrow: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
19.howItsDone: Some people seek awe on purpose: through walks in nature, stargazing, pilgrimages to mountains and great buildings, or by pausing, as the Psalms do, to consider the night sky.

segments.voice: Yesterday: loneliness, and the room is full. Today, a feeling that makes you smaller, in the good way.

The ocean, seen for the first time. A storm rolling in over a field. A night sky far from any city, so full of stars it looks fake. A newborn's hand. Moments like these can stop a person in their tracks. For a second, the self goes quiet. The problems don't vanish; they just get smaller, because something else got very big. And it's easy to go weeks without one, eyes down: on screens, on sidewalks, on lists.
screen: `THE OCEAN, A STORM, THE STARS.` → `FOR A SECOND, THE SELF GOES QUIET.` → `EYES DOWN, FOR WEEKS.`

segments.voice: In 1836, the American writer Ralph Waldo Emerson asked his readers to imagine something: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore". His point is that they do appear, every clear night. The wonder is always on offer, to anyone who looks up. A psalm looked at the same night sky, long before: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Notice the move. Look at the vast thing, and the question comes back to you: how small I am, and how strange that I'm here at all. Now the lab. Researchers who study awe, including the psychologist Dacher Keltner at Berkeley, find it has a signature: people describe feeling small, and it isn't a bad feeling. The self shrinks, and the world opens. In one study, people spent one minute looking up at a grove of very tall eucalyptus trees, while others looked up at a tall building. Then a researcher stumbled and dropped a handful of pens. The people who'd been looking at the trees picked up more of them. One minute of awe, and people were a little more helpful. Some astronauts who've seen the whole earth from space describe a version of this too. An essayist, a psalmist, a lab: very different beliefs about what's behind the stars, and the same move. Look up, and come back down a little different.
screen: `ONE NIGHT IN A THOUSAND YEARS.` · `WHEN I CONSIDER THY HEAVENS.` · `SMALL, AND IT ISN'T BAD.` · `THE TREES AND THE DROPPED PENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can, look out a window, or step outside. Find the biggest thing you can see: the sky, a tree, a building, the clouds. If you're stuck inside, close your eyes and remember the biggest thing you've ever stood under. For about seventy-five seconds, just look. Let it be big. Let yourself be small next to it. You don't need to name what you feel.
Awe. The feeling of standing next to something vast, and getting a little smaller, and a little more generous. Nineteenth word.
Your line: look up. The sky is free, and it's there every night. Day nineteen.

screen: `DAY 19 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY TRADITION SAYS IT: YOU CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.`

20.title: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
20.hook: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
20.howItsDone: Many traditions practice together: Buddhists speak of the sangha and good friendship, Jews gather a minyan for key prayers, Muslims pray in congregation, Sikhs gather as the sangat, and Christians meet as a church.

segments.voice: Yesterday: awe, and look up. Today, the people who make a practice stick.

Anyone who's tried to change a habit alone knows how it goes. Day one, fired up. Day four, a little tired. Day nine, you skip once, then twice, and nobody notices, because nobody knew. Then there are the times something actually stuck. Very often, someone else was in it. A running buddy who'd be standing on the corner at seven. A friend who'd ask, did you do it? A group that noticed when you weren't there. Many of the world's traditions, for all their differences, say it in their own words: you can't do this alone.
screen: `DAY NINE, NOBODY NOTICES.` → `SOMEONE ON THE CORNER AT SEVEN.` → `YOU CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.`

segments.voice: There's a conversation in the early Buddhist texts that surprises people. The Buddha's attendant, Ananda, says that good friendship, having admirable companions, must be half of the spiritual life. The Buddha corrects him. Not half, he says. It's the whole of it. The Hebrew Bible says it plainly: "Two are better than one". And then the picture: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." In Jewish practice, some prayers, like the mourner's Kaddish, are traditionally said only with a minyan, a group of ten. You need other people just to say them. In Islam, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that prayer offered together in congregation is worth many times more than prayer offered alone; one well-known report puts it at twenty-seven times. Sikhs speak of the sangat, the gathered community, and Christians of the church, meaning the gathered people, not only the building. And a long-running study at Harvard has followed hundreds of people for more than eighty years. When its directors are asked what best predicts who stays healthy and happy into old age, their answer isn't money or fame. It's the quality of people's relationships. So a sit on your own with an app is a real start. But each of these homes adds something: find your people.
screen: `NOT HALF. THE WHOLE OF IT.` · `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.` · `A MINYAN, A CONGREGATION, A SANGAT.` · `EIGHTY YEARS OF ONE STUDY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about seventy-five seconds, bring to mind the people who've lifted you up when you fell. One at a time. A face, a name, a moment. Then let one more face come: someone you'd like to walk this path with, even a little. Don't plan anything. Just let them arrive. If you pray, you can hold them there.
Company. The people who lift you up when you fall, and the ones who notice when you're not there. Twentieth word.
Your line: find your people. Someone who notices when you're not there is worth a lot. Tomorrow, camp one closes.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; Rumi's field beyond our ideas of right and wrong (a paraphrase; the well-known wording is a modern, copyrighted version)
21.tomorrow: Marcus doesn't want to get up
21.howItsDone: Rumi's poems are read and sung across the Muslim world and far beyond; in the Mevlevi order founded by his followers, his verses accompany the sema, the turning ceremony people call whirling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: company, and find your people. Today, the last day of camp one.

Three weeks ago you took one breath with a bell. Today you've got twenty words on your strand, and you're standing at the edge of the first camp, looking up at the mountain ahead. So for the last word of camp one, a poet. Not a rule, not a technique. A person. A Persian poet whose lines get shared on phones every day, often with his name on them and his world left off.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.` → `A PERSON, NOT A RULE.`

segments.voice: Jalal al-Din Rumi was born in the eastern Persian world, in what's now Afghanistan or Tajikistan; the old biographies disagree on the town. His family moved west, ahead of the Mongol invasions, and settled in Konya, in today's Turkey. He became a respected Muslim scholar and teacher, steeped in the Qur'an, and his poetry is full of it. Popular versions often leave that out. Then, already a grown man with students of his own, he met a wandering mystic called Shams of Tabriz, and his life turned over. The old biographies say the friendship was so intense that his students grew jealous, and Shams eventually disappeared. Out of that loss came an ocean of poems. His great work, the Masnavi, begins with a reed flute crying. It was cut from the reed bed, and every note it plays is longing to go back. There's a famous saying credited to Rumi about a field, somewhere beyond our ideas of doing wrong and doing right, where he'll meet you. The wording most people share is a modern English version, not his, and scholars aren't sure how closely it follows the Persian. So, paraphrased and honestly labeled: a place past the arguing, where two people can simply meet. That's where camp one has been walking you. Meant to be. Breathe. Memento mori. Namaste. Manifesting. The shadow. Karma. Thoughts. Body. Sit. The phone. Silence. Enough. Gratitude. The golden rule. Kindness. Service. Loneliness. Awe. Company. Rumi. Twenty-one words from many homes, and not one of them asked you to believe anything.
